Thermochemistry

Warm up your skills. Follow the heat, spot the phase change, and build your solution one step at a time.

How to play
  1. Choose a practice mode or use Mixed Practice for a little of everything.
  2. Read the conditions and supplied data. Enter the requested quantity and unit; use a negative q when the sample releases heat.
  3. Choose Check Step to lock in your work. Hints guide you; Show Step reveals the answer and marks the whole problem assisted.
  4. Open the solution map and completed work when needed, or turn on their Always show switches. When finished, choose New Question for a fresh randomized example.

Numeric answers accept ordinary numbers, 2.70 × 10^3, or 2.70E3. Final calculations specify 2, 3, or 4 significant figures; keep extra digits between steps. Some fields require units typed with the number: J, kJ, g, or degC. Follow each field’s instructions.

Choose a skill for guided practice, or take the 10-Question Check for your selected course. Quiz questions may have several steps. Hints and reveals are disabled; your study plan uses retries and skipped questions to recommend review. Quiz results do not change practice XP.

Completed work

    References & hints

    CHEM 1A energy equations
    ΔU = q + w
    w = −PextΔV
    ΔH = ΔU + PΔV (constant pressure)
    qp = ΔH (only PV work)
    qv = ΔU (rigid bomb)
    qcal = CcalΔT
    qrxn = −(qsolution + qcal)
    qhot + qcold = 0
    1 L·atm = 101.325 J
    Hess’s law: equation matching
    1. Compare each given equation with the target.
    2. Reverse an equation when needed and reverse the sign of ΔH.
    3. Multiply or divide every coefficient and ΔH by the same factor.
    4. Add the equations. Cancel equal amounts of identical species on opposite sides.
    5. Add adjusted enthalpies. Check that the remaining equation is the target.
    Formation enthalpy quick table

    ΔH°rxn = ΣnΔH°f(products) − ΣnΔH°f(reactants). Values below are in kJ/mol at 298.15 K. Match the physical state.

    Selected data from OpenStax Chemistry 2e, Appendix G. Elements in their standard states have zero formation enthalpy. C(s) here means graphite.

    Enthalpy stoichiometry

    Balance first. The stated ΔH belongs to the whole equation, not automatically to one mole.

    grams ÷ molar mass → moles
    q = n × ΔH / ν (ν = balanced coefficient of the specified species)

    For a missing formation value, substitute all known coefficient-weighted terms into products − reactants, then solve for the unknown.

    Choose the right equation
    Temperature changes: q = mcΔT
    ΔT = Tf − Ti
    Phase changes: q = nΔH
    Mass to moles: n = m / molar mass
    Multiple stages: qtotal = q₁ + q₂ + …

    Use q = mcΔT on a slope. Use q = nΔH on a plateau at a transition temperature. A pure substance changes phase at constant temperature at a fixed pressure.

    Endothermic: q > 0
    Exothermic: q < 0

    Phase-change recipes
    ChangeNameHeat
    Solid → liquidMeltingAbsorbed
    Liquid → solidFreezingReleased
    Liquid → gasVaporizationAbsorbed
    Gas → liquidCondensationReleased
    Solid → gasSublimationAbsorbed
    Gas → solidDepositionReleased

    Boiling is vaporization at the boiling point. Evaporation also changes liquid to gas, but can occur below the boiling point.

    Reading diagrams and curves
    • Phase diagram: vertical axis is pressure; horizontal axis is temperature.
    • A boundary separates two phases that can coexist in equilibrium.
    • The triple point is where solid, liquid, and gas coexist in equilibrium.
    • A heating-curve slope means temperature is changing within a phase.
    • A plateau means phase change; energy changes intermolecular potential energy rather than temperature.
    • Plateau heat = end heat coordinate − start heat coordinate.

    The phase diagram here is schematic, for a typical substance with a positive solid–liquid boundary slope. It is not water’s phase diagram.

    Substancec, J/(g·°C)

    Units and rearrangements
    1 kJ = 1000 J
    1 cal = 4.184 J
    1 kcal = 1 food Cal = 1000 cal
    m = q / (cΔT)
    c = q / (mΔT)
    Tf = Ti + q/(mc)
    K = °C + 273.15
    °F = 1.8(°C) + 32

    A temperature difference of 1 °C equals a difference of 1 K. Use °C throughout this game.

    🧊 Try it: equal heat, different samples

    Both samples start at 20 °C. Change the masses and materials, then add the same heat to each. This model stays within a single phase and uses constant specific heats; it does not model melting or boiling.

    🔬 Explore PhET: Intro only

    Drag a thermometer onto the objects. Heat or cool water, oil, and blocks; compare their temperature changes. Turn on Energy Symbols and place a warm object in cooler water to follow the energy transfer.

    Think about it: Does equal heating give equal temperature changes? Which way does energy move when objects touch? How does adding more material affect the temperature change?
